# Numbers

BPL has two kinds of number. A bare number such as `0.5` is approximate: a float of the default width, 64 bits unless [`•prefs`](system/prefs.qmd) sets 16 or 32. A number marked with `ₓ`, such as `3ₓ`, is an exact integer, and `1r3` is an exact rational. Comparisons give Booleans, written `$t` and `$f`.

## Writing numbers

| Written | Value |
|---|---|
| `3`, `0.5`, `1E¯3`, `1ₑ¯3` | Approximate numbers. `e`, `E` or `ₑ` writes an exponent |
| `¯2` | A negative number. [`¯`](glyphs/overbar.qmd) is part of the number, and [`-`](glyphs/minus.qmd) is a function |
| `3ₓ` | An exact integer |
| `1r3`, `1ᵣ3` | An exact rational |
| `2j3`, `2J3`, `2ⱼ3` | A complex number, 2 + 3i, with approximate parts |
| `∞`, `¯∞` | [Infinities](glyphs/infinity.qmd) |
| `$n` | NaN |
| `$t`, `$f` | True and false |
| `1.5ₕ`, `1.5ₛ`, `1.5ₚ` | A 16-bit, 32-bit or 64-bit float, whatever the default width |
| `2j3ₛ`, `2j3ₚ` | A complex number with 32-bit or 64-bit parts. `2j3ₕ` has 32-bit parts too |
| `⍬`, `⍬ₓ`, `⍬ₕ`, `⍬ₛ`, `⍬ₚ` | The approximate, the exact, and the 16-bit, 32-bit and 64-bit [empty vector](glyphs/zilde.qmd) |
| `[…]ₓ`, `(…)ₓ` | A list, or rows, in which every number is exact |
| `[…]ₕ`, `[…]ₛ`, `[…]ₚ` | A list, or rows, in which every real number is a 16-bit, 32-bit or 64-bit float, and every complex number has parts of that width, or 32-bit parts after `ₕ` |

A plain `e`, `j` or `r` starts a name unless the rest of a number follows it, as in `1e5`, `1r3` and `2j3`. The subscript forms are always part of the number, and results display with them, as in `1ᵣ3`, `2ⱼ3` and `1ₑ20`.

```bpl
1j2+3j4              ⍝ 4j6
1E¯3                 ⍝ 0.001
¯2+5                 ⍝ 3
2J3≡2j3              ⍝ $t
1ᵣ3≡1r3              ⍝ $t
edges←3 ⋄ 2edges     ⍝ 2 3
```

## Exact and approximate

Exact arithmetic grows as needed. Mixing exact and approximate numbers gives an approximate result. Examples on these pages write `ₓ` for exact input.

```bpl
1÷3                  ⍝ 0.3333333333333333
1ₓ÷3ₓ                ⍝ 1r3
1r3+1r6              ⍝ 1r2
1r2+0.5              ⍝ 1
9223372036854775807ₓ+1ₓ ⍝ 9223372036854775808ₓ
```

A function keeps exact integers exact only if every finite result it gives for them is rational. Arithmetic, `!`, and `*` with an integer exponent keep them exact. `√`, `⍟`, `π`, `○` and monadic `*` give approximate results, whole ones included. An exact function gives the float `∞` at a pole, such as `÷0ₓ`:

```bpl
2ₓ*¯2ₓ               ⍝ 1r4
!20ₓ                 ⍝ 2432902008176640000ₓ
√4ₓ                  ⍝ 2
÷0ₓ                  ⍝ ∞
```

Predicates, positions, tally, shape, and monadic `⌊`, `⌈` and `×` return exact integers. A float beyond the `i64` range floors to an exact big integer:

```bpl
⌊2.5 ¯2.5            ⍝ [2 ¯3]ₓ
⌊2*70                ⍝ 1180591620717411303424ₓ
```

Iota and random integer generation keep an exact argument exact. An argument that must be an integer, such as an index or a count, accepts a float within `1E¯14` of one, whatever the [tolerance setting](system/prefs.qmd):

```bpl
⍳10×0.1×3          ⍝ 0 1 2
```

## Numbers in one array

Numbers that an operation puts in one array share a kind. A float among exact integers makes them all floats, and a complex number makes every number complex:

```bpl
⍳3ₓ , 0.5            ⍝ 0 1 2 0.5
⍳2ₓ , 1j2            ⍝ 0 1 1j2
1ₓ,0.5 ÷ 2ₓ          ⍝ 0.5 0.25
```

Each number written in a literal list or in brackets keeps its own exactness, even beside numbers of the other kind. Floats written beside complex numbers become complex. Their values don't change:

```bpl
1ₓ 0.5÷2ₓ            ⍝ 1r2 0.25
[1ₓ 0.5]÷2ₓ          ⍝ 1r2 0.25
```

Around literals, `[…]ₓ` and `(…)ₓ` make every number exact, at any depth. Each number must be whole. After a list or group that holds anything else, as after a name, `ₓ` is [`⌊`](glyphs/downstile.qmd), as [Superscripts and subscripts](scripts.ipynb) describes. A vector of exact integers displays as `[…]ₓ`, and rows of them as `(…)ₓ`. `⍕` writes them the same way:

```bpl
[1 0 1]ₓ≡1ₓ 0ₓ 1ₓ    ⍝ $t
[[1 2] 3]ₓ≡[1ₓ 2ₓ;3ₓ]   ⍝ $t
(0 1⋄2 3)ₓ≡[[0 1]ₓ [2 3]ₓ]  ⍝ $t
1↑⍬ₓ                 ⍝ [0]ₓ
⍕1ₓ ¯2ₓ              ⍝ "[1 ¯2]ₓ"
```

## Storage

An array keeps its items in one of nine storages: `bool`, `integer`, `float64`, `float32`, `float16`, `complex128`, `complex64`, `character` or `mixed`. `(•storage x).kind` names the storage of `x`. Mixed storage keeps each item's own kind. A literal list of exact and approximate numbers uses it:

```bpl
x←1ₓ 0.5 2ₓ
(•storage x).kind      ⍝ "mixed"
```

Rationals and exact integers beyond 64 bits have no compact storage. An array that holds one uses mixed storage, as does an array that holds numbers together with characters, nested arrays or functions. An imported JSON object is mixed too.

Selecting from, catenating or assigning into mixed storage keeps each item's kind. Arithmetic builds fresh storage from its results, and each result keeps its own kind. Every result of `1×x` is approximate, which makes it a float array. `1ₓ×x` keeps the exact results exact:

```bpl
x←1ₓ 0.5 2ₓ
(•storage 1×x).kind    ⍝ "float64"
(•storage 1ₓ×x).kind   ⍝ "mixed"
```

Boxed display marks mixed storage with `+`, and exact integers with `ₓ`.

Integer storage keeps each item in 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes. One byte holds 0 to 255. Literals, reductions and positions take the fewest bytes that hold every item. Imported buffers preserve supported item widths. Pervasive arithmetic keeps its arguments' size, and moves to the next size up when a result doesn't fit. An exact result beyond 8 bytes becomes a big integer in mixed storage. The size never changes a result, and `•storage` doesn't show it.

## Float widths

Floats come in three widths: 64, 32 and 16 bits. `•storage` gives their kind as `"float64"`, `"float32"` and `"float16"`. [`•float`](system/float.qmd) converts an array to any of them. A 64-bit float holds about 16 significant digits, a 32-bit float about 7 and a 16-bit float about 3. They take 8, 4 and 2 bytes. The largest finite 16-bit float is 65504.

Bare numbers are floats of the default width: 64 bits, or 16 or 32 after [`•prefs`](system/prefs.qmd) `["float":16]` or `["float":32]`. Code parsed after the change reads its numbers at the new width. In a REPL or a notebook, that is the next input. Leading `•prefs` calls on a literal record run before the rest of their code is parsed. A script, a notebook cell, a module or `⍎` text that starts with `•prefs ["float":32]` therefore reads its own numbers at 32 bits. Numbers that `•csv`, `•json` and `•vfi` read also take the default width. So do random numbers, the numbers that `•image` reads, and floats that a function gives from exact arguments, such as `√2ₓ`. Times from `•time` and `•date` are always 64-bit, because a 32-bit float holds seconds since 1970 only to within about two minutes. `ₕ` marks a 16-bit float, `ₛ` a 32-bit float and `ₚ` a 64-bit float, whatever the default. Display marks floats of the other widths, once after an array's notation. `•literal⁻¹` marks every float. Its text therefore reads back the same at any default.

```bpl
{(•storage ⍵).kind}¨[1.5ₕ 1.5ₛ [1.5 2.5]ₚ ⍬ₛ]   ⍝ "float16" "float32" "float64" "float32"
[1.5 2.5]ₛ                          ⍝ [1.5 2.5]ₛ
•literal⁻¹ 0.5                     ⍝ "0.5ₚ"
```

An operation on floats computes at their width. An exact operand rounds to the width that the operation computes at. Floats of two widths compute at the wider. No operation widens floats on its own.

```bpl
v←32 •float 1.5 2.5
{(•storage ⍵).kind}¨[v×2ₓ v×v *v v×2]   ⍝ "float32" "float32" "float32" "float64"
•float v                     ⍝ 32ₓ
(32 •float 1.5)×16777217ₓ    ⍝ 25165824
```

Complex numbers have 64-bit or 32-bit parts. `•storage` gives their kind as `"complex128"` and `"complex64"`, after their whole size. They follow the rules for floats. A complex number takes the width of the floats it comes from, and a 16-bit float that becomes complex takes 32-bit parts. A complex number beside a float computes at the wider of their widths. A complex result with no imaginary part is a float of its parts' width. `ₛ`, `ₚ` and `ₕ` mark the width of the parts, and display marks parts that aren't of the default width:

```bpl
{(•storage ⍵).kind}¨[[2j3]ₛ;[2j3]ₕ;√[¯4]ₛ;[2j3]ₛ×1.5]   ⍝ "complex64" "complex64" "complex64" "complex128"
√¯4ₛ                                       ⍝ 0j2ₛ
```

Each operation on 16-bit floats computes in 32 bits and rounds its result to 16 bits. For `+ - × ÷` and `√`, that gives the result of 16-bit arithmetic. Folds, scans and inner products keep their running totals in 32 bits. Only their results round to 16 bits. A 16-bit total of these numbers would stop growing at 256:

```bpl
+/(16 •float 4096⍴0.1)   ⍝ 409.5ₕ
```

An exact operand converts straight to 32 bits, not to 16. A count larger than 65,504, the largest 16-bit float, still divides a 16-bit sum:

```bpl
h←16 •float 100000⍴1 0
(+/h)÷≢h                 ⍝ 0.49975586ₕ
```

Comparisons of 16-bit and 32-bit floats are always exact. The tolerance that [`•prefs`](system/prefs.qmd) sets applies to 64-bit floats. [`⍣∞`](glyphs/star-diaeresis.qmd) takes two 16-bit or 32-bit results as the same when they lie within 4 units in the last place of each other.

## Infinities and NaN

Floats follow IEEE 754. Besides finite numbers, they include `∞`, `¯∞`, NaN and `¯0`. An undefined result is NaN rather than an error. `1÷0` is `∞`, and `⍟0` is `¯∞`. NaN is written `$n`:

```bpl
[0÷0 ∞-∞]            ⍝ $n $n
[1÷0 ⍟0]             ⍝ ∞ ¯∞
```

Under `=`, NaN equals nothing, as in IEEE. `≡`, search, grade and Key treat NaN as one value, and grade puts it after every other number:

```bpl
$n=$n                ⍝ $f
$n≡$n                ⍝ $t
```

Complex arithmetic follows the `num_complex` crate. A complex number can have infinite or NaN parts.

An infinity or NaN is a float. Joining one to exact integers makes them floats, as any float does:

```bpl
⍳3ₓ , ∞              ⍝ 0 1 2 ∞
(•storage ⍳3ₓ , ∞).kind   ⍝ "float64"
```

CSV and JSON imports give NaN for a missing number. An integer column with gaps then becomes floats. A column that also holds an integer too large for a float to hold exactly keeps each item's kind, in mixed storage.

`⌊` and `⌈` return an exact argument unchanged beside an infinity. Beside NaN they give NaN:

```bpl
3ₓ⌊∞                 ⍝ 3ₓ
3ₓ⌊$n                ⍝ $n
```

Arithmetic with an infinity gives floats.

## Static kinds

Some functions choose a result's kind from their arguments' values. `√¯4` is complex because the argument is negative, `1j0` is a float because its imaginary part is zero, and an exact integer that overflows grows. Under [`•prefs`](system/prefs.qmd) `["kinds":"static"]`, a result's kind follows from the function and its arguments' kinds alone. A fused computation needs that, because it decides each result's kind before it runs. Real arguments give real results, with NaN outside a function's domain, and complex results stay complex. `⌊`, `⌈` and monadic `×` of floats give floats, and integer `÷` gives floats:

```bpl
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
√¯4 9                ⍝ $n 3
0j1×0j1              ⍝ ¯1ⱼ0
⌊2.5 ∞               ⍝ 2 ∞
7ₓ÷2ₓ                ⍝ 3.5
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
```

Integers compute at the width that the `int` pref sets, 64 bits by default, or at a wider integer's width, and wrap where a result doesn't fit. An integer beside a float takes the float's width. Atoms promote as arrays do. A bare literal at the default width widens narrower floats. Exact fractions stay exact, and comparisons keep their tolerance. Under `•prefs ["int":32]`, an exact integer literal that doesn't fit 32 bits is a LIMIT error:

```bpl
•prefs ["kinds":"static"]
9223372036854775807ₓ+1ₓ    ⍝ ¯9223372036854775808ₓ
(•storage (32 •float 1 2)×2).kind     ⍝ "float64"
(•storage (32 •float 1 2)×2ₓ).kind    ⍝ "float32"
•prefs ["kinds":"dynamic"]
```

## Booleans

Comparisons give Booleans. So does every function whose result is a truth value, such as `~`, `∊`, `⍷` and `≡`. `$t` is true and `$f` is false:

```bpl
x←3 1 4 1 5
x>2                  ⍝ $t $f $t $f $t
```

Wherever a number is expected, `$t` is 1 and `$f` is 0. `+/` counts the true items, `#` keeps the items a Boolean mask marks, and a Boolean used as an index selects position 0 or 1:

```bpl
x←3 1 4 1 5
+/x>2                ⍝ 3ₓ
x>2 # x              ⍝ 3 4 5
4>2 ⌷ "no" "yes"     ⍝ "yes"
```

Arithmetic on Booleans gives integers. `∧`, `∨`, `⊽`, `⊼`, `⌊` and `⌈` on two Booleans give a Boolean:

```bpl
$t+$t                ⍝ 2ₓ
$t∧$f                ⍝ $f
```

Boolean storage takes one byte for each item. Boxed display marks it with `$`:

```bpl
(•storage $t $f).kind   ⍝ "bool"
```
